aiOverview.content: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) is a 1990 civil rights law prohibiting discrimination against individuals with disabilities in all areas of public life, including jobs, schools, transportation, and public/private places. It mandates reasonable accommodations in employment (Title I), accessibility in state/local government (Title II), and public accommodations (Title III). Key Provisions and Requirements of the ADA Employment (Title I): Employers with 15 or more employees must provide "reasonable accommodations" to qualified applicants or employees, such as modifying equipment, adjusting schedules, or making facilities accessible, unless it causes "undue hardship". State and Local Government (Title II): Ensures equal access to services, programs, and activities, including public transportation and web/mobile app accessibility. Public Accommodations (Title III): Requires private entities (restaurants, hotels, stores, theaters) to ensure facilities are accessible and to make "reasonable modifications" to policies for people with disabilities. Definition of Disability: Covers individuals with a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits major life activities, those with a record of such impairment, or those perceived as having one. Rights Protected and EnforcementThe ADA protects against discrimination in hiring, promotion, and firing, as well as ensuring equal access to goods and services. Enforcement: Title I is enforced by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), while Titles II and III are enforced by the U.S. Department of Justice. Penalties: Violations can result in lawsuits, court orders to comply, and significant monetary damages or fines (under Title III, penalties can exceed $75,000 for a first violation and $150,000 for subsequent violations). Web AccessibilityThe ADA.gov website now emphasizes that Title II and III regulations include requirements for website and mobile application accessibility to ensure equal access to services.
